title: Present perfect or past simple? — 4 differences
sourceTitle: 'I've done' or 'I did'? - Ask BBC Learning English
description: 4 điểm khác nhau giữa hiện tại hoàn thành và quá khứ đơn: kết quả ở hiện tại, mốc thời gian đã kết thúc/chưa kết thúc, việc vẫn còn đúng đến nay, và trải nghiệm.

segments.text: Present perfect or past simple?
Maryam wants to find out about the differences.
This can be confusing as we use both for past events.
However, the present perfect has more of a link with the present.
Let's look at four main differences to help.
So, we can use both for things that happened in the past.
But if there's a result in the present, we tend to use the present perfect.
Oh, I've lost my phone.
Can you call me? So, I lost my phone in the past, but it is still lost now in the present.
I've lost my glasses. Can you see them anywhere?
However, if there isn't a result in the present, then we generally use the past simple.
The event is firmly in the past.
It doesn't affect our present.
I lost my phone last week, but someone handed it in.
Did you also hear there was a time phrase - 'last week'?
That brings me onto our next difference.
With finished time words like these, we use the past simple.
I bought myself some flowers yesterday.
With unfinished time words, we normally use the present perfect.
Here are some examples. I've bought so many clothes this year.
Careful though, sometimes these time words can be used with the past simple as well.
It depends on how the speaker views this time.
I haven't had coffee today.
I didn't have a coffee today.
So if I say 'I haven't had a coffee today', maybe it's midday.
The day is still happening.
I haven't had coffee today.
Can you make me a coffee, please?
At the end of the day, I might say 'I didn't have a coffee today'.
I used 'today', but I'm thinking of the day as finished.
Off to bed. Next, if the action started in the past but is still true or still happens now, we can use the present perfect.
I've lived in Brighton for eight years, so I moved here eight years ago, but I still live here now.
However, if the action started in the past and finished in the past, I use the past simple.
I lived in New Zealand for four years, so I lived in New Zealand in the past.
But I don't live there now - I live here.
Another example. They've been married for five years.
They got married five years ago, and they are still married today.
It's their anniversary on Sunday.
In this example, they were married for five years.
They are not married now, but they got divorced last year.
Finally, if you want to talk about an experience in your life and we're not saying when,
you can use the present perfect because your life is still happening.
I've seen the Northern Lights.
However, if you want to talk about a specific event in the past, then we use the past simple.
When I visited Iceland, I saw the Northern lights.
So even though I don't say when, we know that it was a time in the past.

title: Present perfect simple or continuous?
sourceTitle: Present perfect simple or continuous? - Ask BBC Learning English
description: "I've chopped the onions" hay "I've been chopping onions"? Năm điểm khác nhau: hoàn thành vs đang tiếp diễn, kết quả vs quá trình, bao nhiêu vs bao lâu, động từ chỉ trạng thái.

segments.text: 'I've done' or 'I've been doing'.
What's the difference? Let's look at this question from Juan.
I want to know: What is the difference between present perfect and present perfect continuous?
Sometimes they can be very similar.
I've worked at the BBC for 8 years.
I've been working at the BBC for 8 years.
So, here, both sentences are correct and they connect the past with the present.
But let's look at five differences.
Using the present perfect simple emphasises that an action is complete.
It has an effect on the present, but the action has finished.
Someone has eaten my chocolates!
They're all gone. Using the present perfect continuous emphasises that the action is ongoing.
Someone has been eating my chocolates.
There's only a few left.
The action may continue in the future.
We use the present perfect simple to focus on the result of an action.
I've chopped the onions. What's next?
So, the result is: the onions are ready.
We use the present perfect continuous to focus on the doing of an action.
I'm not crying - I've just been chopping onions.
So here, the focus is on doing the action itself – the chopping of onions, so doing this action made me cry.
We also use the present perfect continuous when we can see some evidence of an action that happened a short time ago.
The action is completed, but we can still see the evidence.
I've been cooking all day so the kitchen's a mess.
We use the present perfect simple to focus on how many, or how often.
It's rained every day this week.
I've had four coffees today.
We use the present perfect continuous if the focus is on how long – often with phrases like all morning, all day, for ages.
It's been raining all day!
I've been drinking coffee all morning, and I'm still tired!
Careful though: state verbs, we don't normally use in the continuous.
I've been knowing Beth for three years.
I've known Beth for three years.
And finally, we can use the present perfect continuous to emphasise that our situation is temporary.
I've broken my leg, so I've been working from home lately.

title: Past simple or past perfect?
sourceTitle: The past simple and past perfect tenses - English Learners' Questions
description: Dan giải đáp: "When was the last time you ate here?" — khi nào dùng quá khứ đơn, khi nào dùng quá khứ hoàn thành ("the film had already started").

segments.text: OK! This week's learner question comes from Niki from Hungary, who writes: The following sentence has been giving me a headache for weeks now.
Could you please give me the correct answer and justify it?
When was the last time you had eaten ate in this restaurant?
Two weeks ago. Ok, Niki, are you ready?
Here we go. So, in your example it has to be the past simple.
When was the last time you ate in this restaurant?
Two weeks ago. Now the past simple refers to finished periods of time or moments of time.
It refers to a definite past.
So, it’s often used with time adverbials such as: last night, some time ago, in 1985, earlier today,
at six o clock this morning, the last time, the first time, etc etc etc.
And don’t forget that the auxiliary verb is did.
For example: The first time I ever rode a horse was on my 7th birthday.
And the last time was 6 months ago.
The past simple can also be used to refer to repeated past events and past habits and past states.
For example: When I was small, we lived in a cottage by the sea and I played every day on the beach.
Now, the past perfect is formed using had a past participle verb.
And, we use it when we are already discussing the past and wish to refer back to an event that happened before this point.
For example: When I got to the cinema, the film had already started.
Now, the past perfect can also be used with words like after, as soon as, when and once,
but usually only to emphasise that one action is quite separate and independent and has finished before another one.
Remember, everything’s in the past.
So, compare these sentences: When I got out of the car, I bought a parking ticket.
These two are connected. One follows the other.
However, when I had got out of the car, a dog ran over to me.
These two events are unconnected and separate.

title: Future plans: present continuous, going to or will?
sourceTitle: Future tenses: present continuous, 'be going to', 'will' - English Learners' Questions
description: Câu chuyện ở sân bay: "I'm flying to Spain" (đã có vé), "I'm going to fly to Australia" (kế hoạch), "I will fly to Russia" (quyết định tức thời).

segments.text: This week's learner question comes from Christina from Austria, who asks:
Would you be able to explain the difference between "will" and "going to" when talking about the future, please?
Of course, Christina, it’s quite a common question.
I hope this answer helps.
So, there’s a difference between future predictions and future plans and we’re only going to be looking at future plans for the moment.
Please remember that these rules are a rough guide and sometimes native speakers bend or even break them – so be careful.
So, a man goes to the airport.
He’s carrying a suitcase. In the suitcase is a passport, some clothes, some sunglasses and a ticket.
He goes up to the check-in desk and he says to the lady there, “I’m flying to Spain later today.”
Notice this is the present continuous.
That’s for a future arrangement.
It’s called an arrangement because it’s like a plan, but he has the ticket, and the ticket is evidence of the plan.
This means that if the man were to disappear, the airline would still expect him to arrive for the flight.
That’s what the evidence means.
However, the lady behind the check-in desk says “Sorry.
No, that flight’s been cancelled.
But you can fly to Australia or to Russia.”
Well, this is a big decision, so the man goes to the cafe to think about it.
When he comes back he says, “Ok, I’m going to fly to Australia.”
That’s be going to for a future plan.
He’s had time to think about it in the cafe before speaking, but he doesn’t have a ticket so it’s not an arrangement.
But the lady behind the check-in desk says “Sorry!
You took too long in the cafe.
That flight has gone. But you can still fly to Russia.”
So, the man says, “Ok.
I will fly to Russia.”
That’s will for a future based on a decision made at the moment of speaking.”
He makes the decision at that time.
No plan existed before that.
Did you get it? That’s present continuous for a future arrangement.
It’s be going to for a future plan and it’s will for an instant decision made at that moment.

title: The Grammar Gameshow: past continuous
sourceTitle: The Past Continuous Tense - The Grammar Gameshow Episode 9
description: Gameshow ngữ pháp vui nhộn: hai thí sinh "đấu" câu hỏi về thì quá khứ tiếp diễn — was/were + V-ing, "when" vs "while", hành động dài bị cắt ngang.

segments.text: Our first round is a battle round.
Contestants ask each other questions about the past continuous until one of them makes a mistake.
Helen, do you want to start?
Yes, please! That’s a shame!
Greg, you can go first… Oh!
Right! What is the formula for the past continuous?
‘Was’ or ‘were’ ‘verbING’. What do we use the past continuous for?
Actions which are in progress at a past time.
Give me an example. I was eating dinner at 6pm last night.
Do we use the past continuous with state verbs? No, not usually.
Do we usually use the past continuous with repeated actions?
Yes! Oh! That was vicious!
Well played, but Helen, you made a mistake there.
Leslie? Mostly right! The past continuous is used to describe actions that were in progress at a past time.
It is constructed with ‘was’ or ‘were’ and ‘verbING’ - and, being continuous, it does not usually use state verbs.
However, it does not usually describe repeated actions or habits either.
Sorry Helen, that’s the past simple.
Sorry Helen. 20 points to Greg.
Let’s move on to our next round.
Which of these sentences is incorrect and why?
I was walking when I tripped and fell.
I was walking while I tripped and fell.
When I was walking, I tripped and fell.
While I was walking, I tripped and fell.
Trick question! They are all correct.
No, no. B is wrong We don’t use ‘while’ for quick actions.
Wow. You two are really getting into it!
Leslie? We often use the past continuous and past simple together to describe a longer action that is interrupted by a short one.
These actions are connected with time words like ‘when’ and ‘while’.
However, we do not usually use ‘while’ in front of the short action.
So, well done Helen. Well done Helen.
20 points for you! This is exciting. It’s neck and neck!

title: How to choose the correct tense — it's all about aspect
sourceTitle: How to choose the correct tense in English - BBC English Masterclass
description: Mọi thì trong tiếng Anh = thời gian + "aspect" (simple, continuous, perfect). Hiểu "tính cách" của từng aspect để chọn đúng thì.

segments.text: Are you tense about tense?
Well, don't be! In this session's masterclass I'll let you into a little secret of all English tenses - it's all about character. After this.
Ok guys. In this masterclass we're going to get a little bit theoretical, ok?
So try and hold on.
Tenses in English are made up of two things.
A time and an aspect.
Now almost all languages and cultures recognise three times: past, present and future.
But what about an aspect?
An aspect is the character of a verb.
It adds extra information to the verb's meaning and reflects the perception of the speaker.
Now, depending on who you talk to, there are between two and four aspects, but I like to say three.
They are simple, continuous and perfect and all three of them can be used in past, present and future.
The simple aspect is actually not an aspect at all.
It does not modify the verb in terms of its meaning, only in terms of its form.
And this is because, in all cases, the unmodified verb is enough to express exactly the meaning that the speaker wants to say at the time of speaking.
They broadly fall into three categories.
We have the long term general truth.
For example, I like studying English.
We have the instantaneous. For example, I now pronounce you man and wife.
And we have the habitual.
For example, I woke up every day at 6am last year.
The continuous aspect is formed with some sort of be plus verbING.
The focus of this aspect is primarily upon the duration of an event.
All progressive forms contain characteristics of temporariness, unfinishedness or in progress-ness.
The progressive aspect tends to disregard the end of an action and view the event from the centre.
So, an action might be happening at the moment of speaking.
For example, I'm making a video right now.
Or, around a certain time.
For example, before we met I was living in Scotland.
Or, simultaneously when another action occurs.
For example, When you get home, I'll be working in the office
The perfect aspect is formed with some version of have plus the past participle.
Perfect aspects focus on bridging two times together, and connecting events between one time and another, often through relevancy.
An event in the past might be relevant to the present moment.
An event in the future could be connected in some way to the present or the past.
Perfect verb phrases can describe states.
For example, I've loved you since I first met you.
Actions. For example, I will have gone to the gym by the time you get home.
And habits. For example, my father had started work at 9 o'clock every day for the last 20 years.
And of course we can link aspects to create perfect continuous verb phrases.
These combine the forms of their two base aspects.
For example, have plus been plus verbING, and they combine their meanings.
So we can create verb phrases which focus on actions or events with duration with relevancy to more than one time period.

title: The zero conditional — facts, habits & rules
sourceTitle: The zero conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + hiện tại đơn, hiện tại đơn: sự thật khoa học, thói quen cá nhân ("If I don't sleep well, I'm grumpy") và quy định ("If you don't buy a ticket, you get a fine").

segments.text: Hello, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English, and in this video you'll learn how to talk about facts using something called the zero conditional. Let's get started.
Now, we're often taught the zero conditional in the context of scientific facts.
Typical examples are: If you heat water, it boils.
If you mix red and blue paint, you get purple.
And that's true! But how often do you say things like that?
So the best thing for you to do is to hear real people using the zero conditional.
I asked my colleagues: what happens if you don't get a good night's sleep?
If I don't get a good night's sleep, I usually feel quite groggy, grumpy, and I generally can't concentrate very well.
If I don't get a good night's sleep, I can be a little bit spacey, so I don't really pay attention very well.
I find it really hard to know what's going on.
I have to drink lots of coffee, which probably makes it a lot worse.
If I don't get a good night's sleep, I'm not very happy.
Unfortunately, this does happen quite a lot.
So these are still facts.
They're truths about your personal experience, in a general sense, so notice the use of 'usually', 'generally' and 'this happens quite a lot'.
So, for example, Neil is usually quite happy, but if and when he doesn't sleep well - the condition - he isn't very happy.
And this happens quite a lot: it's a general truth.
Let's hear another example. Usually when I finish work, I play guitar.
So if I don't do that, then I kind of feel a bit stressed out maybe.
Here we have two general truths: So in general, when George finishes work, he plays guitar.
And again, in general, if he doesn't play guitar, he feels stressed out.
In a similar way, we can also use the zero conditional to talk about rules and laws.
If you travel on the train without a ticket and the ticket conductor catches you, then you have to pay a fine of £100.
Okay, so, there's a rule in this building and that's that if you don't film in the right place,
they can just come along and stop you.
I think we're in the right place, I think we're OK.
So again, these are like facts, if this happens, this happens.
If you don't buy a ticket, you get a fine, in general.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a zero conditional.
The structure is the present simple in the if-clause, and present simple in the main or result clause.
To recap, the zero conditional is for scientific facts: If you heat water, it boils.
General truths about your personal experience: If I don't sleep well, I'm grumpy in the morning.
And rules and laws: If you don't buy a ticket, you get a fine.

title: The first conditional — likely future situations
sourceTitle: The first conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + hiện tại đơn, will + V: kế hoạch phụ thuộc thời tiết, tàu bị huỷ thì làm gì, và đưa ra dự đoán.

segments.text: Hello, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English and in this video I'll teach you how to talk about likely future situations
and their possible consequences using something called the first conditional. Let's get started.
Let's hear a very common scenario.
I asked Phil about his options for weekend plans and what they depend on.
All the plans I have depend on the weather because I need to do some work in my garden.
I can only do it if it's not raining.
So if it rains, I'll probably just stay inside and watch a film.
If it doesn't rain, I'll be out in the garden, hammering bits of wood.
So, Phil's weekend plans depend on the weather.
If it rains, he'll stay inside and watch a film.
If it doesn't rain, he'll do some work in the garden.
He's considering two likely future situations and talking about his options for both.
Now, most of us at BBC Learning English live in London, and in London,
the Underground trains and the Overground trains are often delayed or cancelled - a very real situation.
So I asked my colleagues: What will you do if your train home from the office is cancelled?
If all the Tubes are cancelled then I will cry and get three buses home.
If the train is cancelled this evening, uh, cry?
If the train is cancelled and I know before boarding the train, then I'll probably just wander around London for a bit.
Or I might get the bus, if there is a bus that I can take to my house.
Notice how George has quite a few conditions to his plans,
so if the train is cancelled and he knows before boarding the train he will wander, or walk around London for a bit.
Or he might get the bus if there is a bus to his house.
Now, because we can use the first conditional to talk about the future, it's also useful for making predictions,
like this one: If electric cars become cheaper, then more people will buy them.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a first conditional.
The structure is the present simple in the if-clause, and will plus a base verb in the main or result clause.
To recap, the first conditional is used for likely future situations and their possible consequences.

title: The second conditional — imagine & give advice
sourceTitle: The second conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + quá khứ đơn, would + V: trúng một triệu bảng, lạc trên đảo hoang, và lời khuyên "If I were you, I'd…".

segments.text: Hello, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English, and in this video we're looking at how to talk about unlikely
or hypothetical situations using something called 'the second conditional'.
Let's get into it. I asked my BBC Learning English colleagues: What would you do if you won a million pounds?
If I won a million pounds, I'd probably buy a nice little house in the countryside.
If I won a million pounds, I'd probably go travelling all round the world.
So, we have an unlikely situation - winning a million pounds.
Sadly, that doesn't happen often.
So, the second conditional is used to imagine an unlikely situation and think about the outcomes of that.
If George won a million pounds, he'd buy a house in the countryside.
Pippa would go travelling around the world.
Let's hear about another hypothetical scenario.
What would you do if you were alone on a desert island?
What would I do if I was alone on a desert island?
If I was alone on a desert island, I think I'd try to find a way to get off the desert island.
If I was alone on a desert island, I think I would be very bad at surviving.
If I were alone on a desert island, I would panic because I wouldn't know how to survive.
I would feel so lonely.
I would try to find any possible tools.
Again, an unlikely situation of being alone on a desert island.
And we're kind of dreaming and imagining: what would I do if I were in that situation?
Next, we can use the second conditional to give advice, starting with "if I were you...",
meaning 'if I were in your position' faced with the same decision or dilemma.
Listen to my colleague give me some advice about a problem.
I've run out of money this month.
If I were you, I'd ask your parents to give you a small loan so you can survive until the end of the month.
Again, this is a hypothetical situation.
"If I were you" is actually impossible - you can't become someone else.
But you're giving advice by saying, this is what I would do if I were in your position.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a second conditional.
The structure is the past simple in the 'if'-clause and 'would' plus a base verb in the main, or result, clause.
To recap, the second conditional is used to imagine an unlikely situation: If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house in the countryside.
To give advice: It's raining outside, so if I were you, I'd take an umbrella.

title: The third conditional — a different past, regrets, blame
sourceTitle: The third conditional - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + quá khứ hoàn thành, would have + V3: tưởng tượng quá khứ khác đi, nói về tiếc nuối ("I wish I'd…") và đổ lỗi ("If you'd told me…").

segments.text: Hello, this is Georgie from BBC Learning English, and in this video,
we're looking at how to imagine a different past using something called the third conditional. Let's get started.
I interviewed my colleagues in the office.
First, I asked them how they got to work.
I got to work today by bus and then tube.
So Neil is at the office.
He arrived on the underground train - the tube.
But I asked him to think back and imagine a different scenario.
What would you have done if the tube had been cancelled?
Well, if the tube had been cancelled, I would've got a bus a bit further, and then got a train.
So again, Neil arrived at the office successfully on the tube because the tubes were not cancelled, but we're imagining a hypothetical situation where the tubes were cancelled,
and Neil has to imagine the consequences of that and what he would have done instead.
Now, Phil took the overground train to work, but I asked him what he would have done if the trains had been cancelled,
and Phil's response is very fast, but you've got the subtitles there to help you.
If the train had been cancelled, I would've got a different train which takes -
which means I'd have to get two trains and it takes about an extra fifteen, twenty minutes.
Quick note on pronunciation there.
So usually we shorten 'I would have got' to 'would've got', but Phil shortens it even more to 'I woulda got'.
So the third conditional is for imagining a different past, which means it's useful for talking about regrets.
Things we wish we could change about the past.
I asked my colleagues what they regretted.
So I had a friend in primary school and now she has children, but I'm not in touch with her.
So yeah, I wish that I'd stayed in touch with her.
If I'd stayed in touch with her, then I would've known her children.
It would've been nice to know her kids, but I don't.
Beth says she wishes she'd stayed in touch with her friend
because if she had stayed in touch with her friend, she would've known her children.
So we have a typical third conditional structure with an if-clause and a result clause.
And then we have this other common structure where we use 'wish' to express that we want something to be different.
Let's hear more examples. This is a regret that a lot of people probably have, but I wish I had studied harder at school.
I wish I'd travelled to more countries on my gap year.
Lastly, we can use the third conditional to blame someone for something they did.
Why weren't you at the meeting?
Because you didn't tell me about it.
If you'd told me about it, I would've been there.
George is saying that it's Andrew's fault that he didn't go to the meeting, because Andrew didn't tell George about the meeting.
Now, pause the video and think about which structures are used to make a third conditional.
In the if-clause, we use the past perfect, and in the result clause we use 'would' plus 'have' plus a past participle.
To recap, the third conditional is for imagining a different past: If the trains had been cancelled, I would have got the bus.
To talk about your regrets: If I'd had piano lessons, I would have learnt how to read music.
And, to assign blame: If you'd told me about the meeting, I would've been there.

title: Mixed conditional — past cause, present result
sourceTitle: Mixed conditional 1 - Grammar: Conditionals with Georgie
description: If + quá khứ hoàn thành, would + V: việc trong quá khứ ảnh hưởng hiện tại — "If I'd slept properly, I wouldn't be so tired now."

segments.text: Hi, I'm Georgie from BBC Learning English and maybe you've heard of conditionals - the zero, the first, the second, the third.
But did you know that you can mix them up to have new meanings? Let's take a look.
Now, we could say that our lives now are a result of a chain of events that happened in the past.
I live in London now because I applied for a job in the past.
Neil has another example of this.
I am so tired. I hardly slept last night.
If I'd slept properly, I wouldn't be so tired now.
So, Neil is tired now.
Why? Because he didn't sleep well in the past.
Now, this is a type of mixed conditional.
You might recognise the third conditional structure in the first part and the second conditional structure in the second part,
but we'll come back to the structure later.
For now, you just need to know that this type of mixed conditional is for expressing how your life now is affected by something that happened in the past.
Let's hear more examples. If I hadn't got this job, I would probably still be in Korea.
George used to live in South Korea.
Does he live there now?
No, he lives in London, working for the BBC.
Again, he's imagining how a past event influenced his present reality.
He got the job in the past, so now he lives in London, not Korea.
Let's hear from Pippa. So if Covid hadn't happened, I wouldn't live where I live now
because I wouldn't be able to work from home and I wouldn't be able to live outside of London.
Since the pandemic, a lot more people are able to work from home.
Now Pippa's job is in London, but because of the pandemic,
she's able to live outside of London because she doesn't have to come into the office every day.
Something in the past is affecting her life now.
What about Buli and Phil?
If I hadn't learnt Spanish when I was younger, my life would be very different now.
If I hadn't got married, I wouldn't be working in London right now.
OK, now you know when to use it.
But how do you use it?
Pause the video and think about which structures are used to make this type of mixed conditional.
The structure is the past perfect in the 'if' clause and 'would' plus a base verb in the main or result clause.
To recap, this mixed conditional is about how past events are affecting your life now.
If I had eaten breakfast, I wouldn't be so hungry now.
